new_statements.rule_in_words: Vietnamese (a contour-tone language) has no culminative word-stress system; stress in the literature is phrase-level accentual prominence. Instrumentally, in disyllabic reduplications spoken utterance-medially in a fixed carrier sentence by 10 Saigon speakers, the second (base) syllable is more prominent than the first (reduplicant): longer, larger F0 range and fuller tone shape, less vowel centralisation, less spectral tilt; tone sandhi is confined to the weak first syllable. The authors conclude that if these words have a stress pattern it is right-headed (final), explicitly not attributable to final lengthening, but leave open whether the unit is a stress foot or a phonological word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none discussed (disyllabic domain only: weak first syllable, strong second syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone sandhi occurs only in a subset of reduplications and only on first syllables; Southern speakers merge hỏi and ngã (5 tones), which conditions which sandhi forms exist; no lexical exceptions to the right-headed pattern are reported.
new_statements.identity_note: MKS 37 (work 1): 10 speakers of Southern Vietnamese, Saigon dialect (5 tones, hỏi/ngã merged). new_statements.rule_in_words: No lexical (contrastive) word stress: compounds and their homophonous phrases are produced and perceived identically by Hanoi, Hue and Saigon speakers unless speakers deliberately insert a juncture (phrase-level strategy); there is no English-type compound-stress rule. But within disyllabic words (reversible coordinative compounds in a constant carrier sentence) the second syllable is phonetically more prominent (longer, larger F0 range, fuller tone, higher F1), i.e. a right-headed (final) prominence that the authors treat as a phonetic tendency on which no phonological contrast depends. No significant dialect difference in the compound/phrase result; the right-headed asymmetry held across the three dialects (curve-tone F0 effects strongest for Southern speakers).
new_statements.exceptions: Hanoi speakers lengthened both syllables of phrases relative to compounds (a dialect-specific production detail) but were no better at perceiving the contrast; intensity was marginally LOWER on the prominent second syllable; the compound/phrase comparison could not test syntagmatic prominence, hence Experiment 3.

readall_conflicts: No outright contradiction of the catalog's no-word-stress coding: both Nguyen & Ingram papers now read in full state that Vietnamese has no system of lexical/culminative word stress and that compounds are prosodically indistinguishable from phrases (all three dialects, including Saigon). They do, however, report a phonetic right-headed (second/final-syllable) prominence inside disyllabic words (coordinative compounds, JASA 2007a; reduplications by 10 Saigon speakers, MKS 37), measured utterance-medially in carrier sentences and explicitly argued not to be final lengthening. That sits in tension with the catalog source's (Brunelle 2017) suggestion that the final prominence previously observed 'may exclusively be due to phrase-final lengthening', and it sides with Thompson 1965 and the Schiering, Bickel & Hildebrandt 2010 statement held by the project (final syllable strong by default in a 2-3-syllable domain). The authors themselves call it a phonetic tendency on which no phonological contrast depends and leave the foot/prosodic-word status open, so the disagreement is about the phonetic source of final prominence, not about the absence of contrastive word stress. Henderson 1966 remains unread (lending-only), so its position is unknown.
